title: Left Over From Before
core: All three describe something that is still here after most of the whole has gone — a survivor of some process of loss, decay, removal, or extinction. Each looks backwards and quietly implies an absent majority. They split on what they claim about the survivor: whether it still works, how much of it there is, and whether the rest was destroyed or merely used up.
exam_note: The test swaps in **vestigial** where the sentence only claims survival, not uselessness — check whether the sentence actually says the thing stopped doing its job before you accept it.

words.nuance: The only one that asserts **uselessness** — it is a verdict on function, not on quantity. A vestigial thing is still fully present and can even be conspicuous (a whole tailbone, a veto still written into the charter); what it has lost is its job. Say **vestigial** and you have diagnosed something as an evolutionary hangover.

The only one that is a **measured quantity** — what a process left behind after consuming the bulk, and the one word here that can be a noun and take a number. It says nothing about being broken: **residual** heat still burns you, **residual** resentment still poisons dinner. Its home is engineering, medicine, accounting, statistics.

Claims **existence only** — not lost, not destroyed, not extinct — and is silent on both function and amount. Its implied opposite is *extinct* or *lost*, never *used up*, so the rest of the set was wiped out rather than consumed. It attaches to whole intact survivors that scholars count: manuscripts, species, colonies, the three surviving letters.
